# Invert colors

- Route: `/tools/invert-image-colors`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `invert-image-colors`

## Summary

Flip every pixel to its negative, as a non-destructive layer you can mask, blend or undo. (Photo editing)

## Details

Inverting an image replaces every color with its opposite: black becomes white, a deep blue sky becomes a warm orange, and a scanned film negative becomes a viewable positive. In Aperture this is the Invert entry of the Effects panel, an adjustment layer in the gamma-space stage of the stack that computes 1 minus each channel of the sRGB-encoded pixel. Because it is a layer rather than a destructive filter, you can mask it to a region, lower its opacity for a partial inversion (at exactly 50 percent every pixel lands on mid-gray), set its blend mode to luminosity to flip tones while keeping hues, or stack it below Levels and Curves to finish a negative conversion. The same panel holds Posterize, Threshold and Gamma, which combine naturally with an inversion.
### What it does
- Adds an Invert layer from the Effects panel that maps each channel to 1 minus its value, turning the photo into its exact negative.
- Accepts a mask so only a selected area, a luminosity range or a color range is inverted while the rest stays as shot.
- Supports opacity and the normal, luminosity and color blend modes, which gives partial, tone-only or hue-only inversions.
- Stacks with Levels, Curves and the other Effects entries so an inverted film scan can be color-corrected in the same project.
- Exports the inverted result from the original at full resolution as JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF with metadata kept or stripped.
### How to use it
1. Drop a photo: The editor opens on the Effects panel with the image decoded in the browser.
2. Add Invert: Choose Invert in the Effects panel; the preview flips to the negative immediately.
3. Refine: Optionally add a mask, lower the opacity, or stack Levels and Curves above to correct a film scan.
4. Export: Pick a format and size; the server renders the original with the same inversion.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- Alpha is preserved; only the three color channels are inverted.
- TIFF scans and BMP files need an account for an editable preview copy; JPG and PNG scans decode in the browser.
### Technical details
- The formula is out = 1 - c for each of red, green and blue, on sRGB-encoded values between 0 and 1; there is no luma term, no gamma change and nothing to clamp because the input is already in range. In 8-bit terms a value v becomes 255 - v.
- Inverting twice returns the original exactly in the float pipeline, since 1 - (1 - c) = c, and within rounding in the exported file: the server renders in float64 for images up to 4 megapixels and float32 above that, so a double inversion differs from the source by at most one 8-bit level after encoding.
- A layer opacity below 100 percent mixes the input and the negative, so 50 percent opacity maps every pixel toward 0.5 gray: a value of 0.2 becomes 0.5 and so does 0.8. Luminosity blend keeps the original hue and chroma and takes only the inverted luma; color blend does the reverse.
- Order matters for film scans: the orange mask of a color negative is a global cast, so an Invert layer first, then Levels with per-channel input black and white points set from the histogram, then Curves gives the standard conversion with no second pass.
- Your GPU (WebGL2) draws the inverted preview from a 1920 px copy of the photo; on export our server renders the original at full resolution with the same subtraction, and the two results agree within a small documented tolerance, a few 8-bit levels at most for color stages and exact for grain.
### When not to use it
Inverting is the wrong tool when a photo merely looks too dark or has a color cast; fix exposure with the Basic panel and casts with white balance or color balance instead. A black and white conversion with channel sliders gives far more control over tonality than inverting a desaturated image, and for diagrams that should be white on black with crisp edges, a Threshold layer after inversion usually does more work than the inversion itself.
### Use cases
- Convert a photographed film negative: Invert the frame, then set input black and white per channel in Levels to remove the orange base, and finish with a curve.
- Dark-mode versions of diagrams: Invert a white-background chart or sketch for a dark slide, then threshold it if the scan is gray rather than black.
- Solarization effects: Add a luminosity mask so only the highlights flip, for a Sabattier-style look; a plain 50 percent opacity would turn the whole frame mid-gray instead.
- Checking a composite for seams: A temporary inverted layer makes brightness mismatches along a pasted edge easier to see; delete it before export.
### FAQ
Q: Is inverting the same as making a negative?
A: Yes. Each channel becomes 1 minus its value, which is what a negative is: 8-bit (51, 51, 51) becomes (204, 204, 204), and the sky color (89, 140, 217) becomes a warm (166, 115, 38).
Q: If I invert twice do I get the original back?
A: Exactly in the preview and in the float render, because 1 - (1 - c) is c. The exported file can differ by at most one 8-bit level from the source after re-encoding, and a lossy JPG export adds its own compression noise on top.
Q: Can I invert only part of a photo?
A: Add a mask to the Invert layer: a brush, a gradient, a radial, a luminosity range, a color range or a subject mask all work, and the mask can be feathered and inverted itself.
Q: Why does my inverted negative still look orange or blue?
A: Color negative film has an orange base that inverts to a blue cast. Add a Levels layer above the inversion and set the input black and white points per channel from the histogram; that neutralizes the base without affecting the inversion.
Q: What else is in the Effects panel?
A: Posterize (2 to 255 levels per channel), Threshold (black or white by luma at a chosen level) and Gamma (a power curve from 0.1 to 10). They are separate layers and can be stacked with Invert in any order.
Q: Will inverting change transparency?
A: No. The alpha channel of a PNG or WebP is untouched; only red, green and blue are flipped, so a transparent background stays transparent.
